newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia investor rights win could pave way for more.
newsitem.headline: Russia investor rights win could pave way for more.

text.p: Victories claimed by investors over management at Russian Novolipetsk metals combine (NLMK) in a prominent shareholders rights case could set the stage for many more such cases to be fought out in court, analysts said.

In a battle closely watched as a litmus test of Russian attitudes to the rights of outside and minority investors, three international investment funds which hold stakes in NLMK won favourable rulings from a regional court in recent weeks.

After earlier rulings in favour of Renaissance Capital's Sputnik Fund and Bank MFK, associated with Russia's powerful Uneximbank, the Lipetsk arbitration court last week told plant managers to include nominees from Monaco-based hedge fund Cambridge Capital Management on a list of candidates to be voted on to the board of directors.
Cambridge Capital Management owns 17.2 percent, Bank MFK 15 percent and the Sputnik Fund nine percent of shares in the steelmill.
"It's very good news for shareholders that minority shareholders won the case in a regional court in Lipetsk," said one analyst who asked not to be named.
Some of the plaintiffs said NLMK management used tactics ranging from locking them out of rooms to escorting them off plant grounds to obstruct their attempts to submit nominees.
But senior managers at the plant, who were not available for comment on Wednesday, have said in the past they acted only in accordance with company rules for dealing with investors.

AO Novolipetsky Metallurgichesky Kombinat, Russia's biggest steel producer and located only a few hundred kilometres from Moscow, is not the only former Soviet enterprise to find itself the focus of foreign investor worry.

Regional utility Mosenergo was recently forced under pressure from foreign investors to drop a proposal to issue new shares from the agenda of the annual shareholders meeting, but says it will reconsider the issue at a later date.

And officials at Sibneft, the majority shareholder of oil company Noyabrskneftegaz have not explicitly ruled out the possibility that a planned massive capital increase could lead to a dilution of existing shareholdings.

Sibneft says current shareholders will receive new shares in proportion with their holdings, if shares are issued as part of a capital revaluation, but the timing and other terms of issues will be at the discretion of Noyabrskneftegaz's board.
Some analysts say such problems are all too common.

"The concern I have had is that with the new issues we have seen, existing shareholders have not been given a chance to participate and shares have been diluted," said a Western analyst who also wished to be unnamed.
But others said problems between management and shareholders often get glossed over or swept under the carpet through the desire of one or both sides to avoid open conflict.

"There are very few cases where management is openly hostile to outside investors -- but that's been the case as long as the minority remained silent," said Nikolai Klekovkin, Deputy CEO of Credit Suisse Investment Funds.
"In Russia's case we have seen mostly passive shareholders. This one of the first cases (of active investors). I think we will see more cases like this in the future."

Russian securities and other laws are slowly taking shape and while the new reformist government is seen on the side of investors, there are still many loopholes in legislation which Soviet-era managers can use to confound the unwary.
Overseas investors have typically avoided Russian courts, many of which are still emerging from the Cold War era of show trials and rulings determined by political influence.
But analysts said the outcome of the Novolipetsk hearings should encourage investors to take their complaints to court.
"I think shareholders should be more proactive in asserting their rights," said Ivan Mazalov, analyst at CentreInvest Group.

"If portfolio investors represented by local brokerages want issuers to comply with laws and regulations then they should set up precedents, and sue formally in court. Unless that happens, violations that are not penalised give rise to more violations."
